gaps.discriminates: Acute bilateral labyrinthitis vs. autoimmune inner ear disease (AIED) vs. atypical Ménière’s — AIED often shows rapidly progressive, down-sloping or flat SNHL; viral labyrinthitis more commonly affects high frequencies initially, though bilateral flat loss can occur.

Cochlear (labyrinthitis) vs. retrocochlear (e.g., bilateral vestibular schwannomas — though MRI negative, very small lesions may be missed; or inflammatory neuropathy) — poor speech discrimination out of proportion to pure-tone loss suggests retrocochlear involvement.

True bilateral vestibular hypofunction (supporting labyrinthitis) vs. central compensation masking peripheral deficits, or asymmetric involvement suggesting evolving unilateral disease — vHIT/VEMP quantify canal/saccular function objectively and distinguish BVH from central mimics.

- No fluctuating or episodic pattern — argues against Ménière’s.  
- No unilateral predominance — argues against typical vestibular neuritis or early Ménière’s.

[GAPS]  
- Pure-tone audiogram configuration (e.g., high-frequency vs. flat, symmetric vs. asymmetric) — critical to confirm sensorineural etiology and pattern.  
- Speech discrimination scores and tympanometry — needed to distinguish cochlear vs. retrocochlear vs. middle ear contribution.  
- vHIT and VEMP results — to objectively quantify bilateral semicircular canal and saccular function and confirm vestibular hypofunction.  
- Viral serologies (e.g., CMV, HSV, VZV, EBV) or CSF analysis — not obtained, but would strengthen viral etiology if positive (though rarely clinically pursued).  
- Serial audiometry — to determine if hearing loss is stable or progressive (key for distinguishing from AIED).

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute bilateral labyrinthitis
